chunks: How switching frequency affects performance. The question: How does switching frequency impact performance?
Switching frequency is how many times per second a buck completes its on-off cycle. Raising it shrinks the ripple and lets you use smaller parts.
It also lets the control loop be faster. The price is more heat, since every cycle costs a bit of energy.
A flickering light at 10 flashes per second looks jumpy. At 1,000 flashes per second it looks perfectly steady, so you need almost no smoothing.
But each flash takes effort to produce, so more flashes cost more total effort. Frequency in a buck works the same way: faster switching is smoother, but each flash is not free.

55 amps of ripple, more than the 2 amps load, which would push the converter into DCM.
Switching frequency ( f sw ): switching cycles per second. Ripple current: the inductor's up-and-down swing, which falls as 1 over f sw ("What sets the inductor current slope").
Switching loss: energy wasted per transition, so it grows with f sw . Crossover frequency: the speed of the control loop; it is usually kept well below f sw .
Minimum on-time: the shortest pulse the controller can make.
Take a buck with a 1 amps ripple current at 500 kilohertz. Double the frequency to 1 megahertz with the same inductor, and the ripple current halves to 0. 5 amps.
So you could instead halve the inductor and keep the same ripple current, and the capacitor can shrink too. But if switching loss is 0. 2 watts at 500 kilohertz, it is about 0.
4 watts at 1 megahertz. That is the whole idea.
"Higher switching frequency means less ripple and smaller inductors and capacitors, and it lets the loop be faster.
The cost is that every per-cycle loss, like gate charge, switch-node capacitance and transition overlap, scales linearly with frequency, so efficiency and heat get worse.
It also pushes against the minimum on-time limit for big step-downs and moves your EMI harmonics around.
So you pick a frequency that balances size, efficiency and noise for the application."
